# Standard Operating Procedure

`admin.obj.core.sop` · v1.0.0 · **draft** · scope **core**

> A written, ordered procedure for a recurring task: what starts it, the steps, who performs each one, which systems are touched, where judgement is required, what comes out, and what to do when the happy path fails. An SOP exists to move a process out of one person's head and into a form the organisation owns. It succeeds only to the extent that the written version and the performed version are the same thing, and that equivalence is not a property of the document — it is a claim about the world that decays from the moment of approval and has to be re-established by observation.


**The discriminator.** Could a competent person who has never performed this task complete it correctly from this document alone, without asking anyone? If yes, it is an SOP. If it only tells them what outcome is required or what standard applies, it is a Policy. The test is executability by a stranger, not the presence of numbered paragraphs.


Also called: `SOP`, `Work Instruction`, `Runbook`, `Process Document`, `Desk Instruction`, `Method Statement`, `Standard Work`


### Questions this object answers

- If the person who normally does this were unavailable tomorrow, could anyone else run it?
- Is the written procedure still what we actually do, and when did anyone last check?
- Which of these steps exist to get the work done and which exist to satisfy a control?
- Where in this procedure do the errors happen, and is that step written or assumed?
- What did the new joiner follow last month, and was it the current version?
- What breaks in this process when the named owner leaves in six weeks?
- Is this a procedure at all, or a judgement we have dressed as one?


### What it is NOT responsible for

- Not the rule the procedure serves — that is admin.obj.core.policy. A policy sets the standard; an SOP is one of possibly several ways of meeting it, and may be rewritten entirely without the policy changing a word.

- Not the controlled artefact carrying the text — that is admin.obj.core.document, which owns version, approval block, classification and retention. The SOP is the procedure; the document is how we prove which wording was in force in March.

- Not a single occurrence of the work — that is admin.obj.core.action_item or admin.obj.core.request. Running an SOP a hundred times produces a hundred of those and one of these.

- Not the external duty behind a regulated procedure — that is admin.obj.core.compliance_obligation. The duty says the thing must be done and evidenced; the SOP is our chosen method, and choosing a worse method does not breach the duty until the outcome does.

- Not a checklist. A checklist assumes the performer already knows the process and is guarding against omission under load. An SOP assumes they do not. Filing one as the other is how an organisation discovers, during a handover, that it has nine checklists and no procedures.

## States

Initial `draft` · terminal `superseded`, `archived`

| State | Means | Entered when | Implies |
|---|---|---|---|
| `draft` | Being written or rewritten. Binds nobody and should be followed by nobody, however widely circulated. | — | The process is currently running on tribal knowledge whatever the document says. |
| `pending_approval` | With the approver. Only meaningful where criticality is regulated or safety_critical. | — | The steps are settled; the authority to publish them is not. |
| `approved` | Signed off but not yet effective or not yet communicated to performers. | — | Two versions are legitimately in play. This is the window where handover errors cluster. |
| `published` | Communicated and effective. Not yet evidence of anything about practice. | — | The organisation can now be judged against this wording. |
| `active` | Published, executed and verified against practice. The only state in which the procedure is genuinely doing its job. | `exists: thread.last_inbound` | A stranger could run this task. The bus factor has actually moved. |
| `at_risk` | In force but drifting — verification stale, maintenance overdue, or the systems underneath it changed. | `days_since(commitment.due_at) > 0` | Still being followed, and the people following it are the ones who cannot tell it is wrong. |
| `on_hold` | Deliberately suspended — the system it describes is mid-migration and the steps are known to be temporarily wrong. | — | Better than at_risk despite sounding worse. A suspended procedure sends the performer to a human; a drifted one sends them confidently into the wrong screen.  |
| `superseded` | A newer version is in force. The old wording still governs work performed while it stood. | — |  |
| `archived` | Retired with a recorded reason. Retiring without recording why is how a procedure returns in three years, reconstructed from memory. | — |  |

## Preconditions

- **`sop.process_actually_recurs`** The task is genuinely recurring and someone currently performs it. _(unmet → Block. Do not author. A procedure written for a process nobody runs will be found by search, followed by a joiner, and be wrong — and it will have a current review date, because nothing triggers review on a process that never happens.
)_
- **`sop.a_performer_is_observable`** At least one person who currently performs the task is identified and available to be watched. _(unmet → Degrade, do not block. Author backwards from the output artefacts and the system trail, and cap drift_state at presumed_current with verification_method = owner_assertion. An SOP written from a manager's description is a description of the process the manager believes is happening, which is a genuinely different document.
)_
- **`sop.owner_is_a_named_person`** Ownership resolves to a named individual, with the owning role recorded alongside. _(unmet → Block publication. Route to the function head to name someone, not to the function. A departmentally owned procedure is reviewed by whoever is least busy, and nobody is least busy.
)_
- **`sop.governing_rule_resolved`** Where the procedure serves a policy or an external duty, that link is resolved before the steps are written. _(unmet → Degrade. Author the steps and leave control_steps empty, but flag it: a procedure that does not know which of its steps are controls cannot tell an editor which ones may be simplified away, and the first efficiency review will remove them because they are precisely the steps that do not help finish the work.
)_
- **`sop.tooling_is_not_mid_migration`** The systems the procedure names are stable, not part-way through a replacement. _(unmet → Hold at on_hold rather than publishing. Publishing against a tool being replaced next quarter guarantees the first version anyone reads is the wrong one, and it burns the credibility that makes the second version get read at all.
)_
- **`sop.criticality_is_set`** The consequence of performing this wrongly is classified before any change control is applied. _(unmet → Default to routine and say so. Applying regulated-grade change control uniformly is how organisations end up routing a typo fix in the stationery procedure through the same gate as a sterilisation procedure, which teaches everyone that the gate is theatre.
)_
- **`sop.version_in_force_is_determinable`** The wording in force on a given date can be established from the record. _(unmet → Block any use of the procedure as evidence — of training, of control operation, of what the joiner was told. Version identity has to live on the copy the performer opened, not only on the master, and almost nowhere does.
)_


## Constraints

- **`sop.cannot_contradict_its_policy`** A procedure cannot permit what the policy it implements forbids. Where they conflict the procedure is defective, not the policy negotiable.
- **`sop.cannot_bind_conduct_before_effective_from`** Work performed before effective_from is judged against the version then in force, never against the current one.
- **`sop.regulated_change_requires_approval`** Where criticality is regulated or safety_critical, no step change takes effect without recorded approval by the named approver.
- **`sop.control_step_removal_needs_the_control_owner`** A step marked as a control may not be removed by the process owner alone.
- **`sop.cannot_evidence_its_own_execution`** The existence of the procedure is never evidence that it was followed.
- **`sop.stranger_test_before_publication`** A business_critical or higher procedure should not be published until someone who has never performed the task has completed it from the document. _(soft)_
- **`sop.deviation_recorded_or_it_is_a_change`** A departure from the written steps is either a recorded deviation or an unapproved change to the procedure. There is no third category.


## Business rules

- **`sop.no_publish_without_named_owner`** A procedure with no named individual owner may not reach published. — _Departmental ownership is the same as no ownership with better optics._
- **`sop.material_change_requires_reissue`** A change to a step, its order, or its performer is a new version with a new effective date, not an edit to the existing one. Correcting a typo is an edit; correcting a step is a reissue.
 — _Silent step edits destroy the only useful property of version control — the ability to say what the person in front of you was told to do.
_
- **`sop.superseded_must_be_withdrawn`** On supersession, the previous version must be removed from every location performers look, not merely marked superseded in a register.
 — _A superseded procedure still in the shared drive is followed by exactly the people the register was supposed to protect — the ones who do not know there is a register.
_
- **`sop.regulated_change_needs_approval`** A step change to a regulated or safety_critical procedure without recorded approval is void, not provisional.
- **`sop.deviation_needs_a_record`** Every departure from the written steps carries a timestamp, a performer and a reason, recorded at the time rather than reconstructed. — _Contemporaneous recording is the whole of the ALCOA+ principle and the whole of its value. A deviation reconstructed at audit is a story about a deviation.
_
- **`sop.overdue_verification_downgrades_assurance`** Past its verification date the procedure may not be cited as an operating control. It may still be followed; it may not be relied on.

- **`sop.single_performer_flags_continuity_risk`** A business_critical or higher procedure with one performer carries a continuity risk flag regardless of how well it is written. — _The quality of the document is not the risk. The absence of a second person is._
- **`sop.presumed_current_is_not_verified`** drift_state = presumed_current may never be reported as verified, and a review with verification_method = owner_assertion does not advance it.
 — _This is the rule that stops a document-control system reporting a wholly unchecked procedure set as green, which is what every such system does by default.
_
- **`sop.tribal_only_is_not_coverage`** A procedure with readability = tribal_only does not count towards documented-process coverage, however complete its metadata. — _The metadata is complete. The procedure does not exist._


## Exceptions — where the rules above are legitimately wrong

- **Under a live incident a performer may depart from the written steps and record the deviation afterwards rather than seeking approval first.
** — A procedure that cannot be departed from under fire is departed from permanently instead of temporarily, and the departure is never recorded because recording it would have required admitting the first breach. The after-the-fact record is what keeps the deviation an input to the next revision rather than a private amendment.
 _(overrides sop.deviation_recorded_or_it_is_a_change, sop.regulated_change_needs_approval)_
- **In safety_critical and most regulated procedures the emergency deviation right does not exist. The work stops rather than proceeding off-procedure.
** — Aviation and pharmaceutical manufacturing both settled here independently and for the same reason: the expected cost of an unrecorded deviation exceeds the cost of a stopped line. The exception to the exception matters because a single deviation policy applied across a mixed procedure set is wrong at one end or the other.
 _(overrides sop.emergency_deviation_with_after_record)_
- **Where a named system is unavailable, a documented workaround temporarily replaces the affected steps and expires with the incident.
** — Undated workarounds become the procedure — this is how half of any long-lived process set was actually written. The expiry date is the entire control; without it the workaround outlives the outage, the outage is forgotten, and nobody can explain why the step exists.
 _(overrides sop.material_change_requires_reissue)_
- **A genuinely judgement-heavy process may legitimately be captured as principles and worked examples rather than as steps, and marked readability = narrative deliberately.
** — Some processes are decisions wearing a procedure's clothes — handling a distressed complainant, deciding whether a spend is capital. Writing steps for them produces a document that will be followed literally by exactly the person least equipped to notice it is the wrong call. The honest admission that this one needs an experienced person is more useful than a procedure that manufactures false confidence.
 _(overrides sop.tribal_only_is_not_coverage)_
- **Where two sites operate under different jurisdictions or different systems, a local variant is correct and the single-source rule does not apply.
** — Forcing one document across two legal regimes produces a document that is wrong in one of them and is followed in both. The requirement in this case is a variant register with a named owner per variant, not consolidation.
 _(overrides sop.superseded_must_be_withdrawn)_
- **A procedure that is the subject of an investigation, claim or regulatory enquiry is not amended until the matter closes, even where it is known to be wrong.
** — Amending it mid-enquiry reads as an admission and destroys the ability to establish what was in force. The correct move is a documented interim instruction to performers plus a recorded reason the review lapsed — not a quiet edit and not a pretence that the procedure is fine.
 _(overrides sop.material_change_requires_reissue, sop.overdue_verification_downgrades_assurance)_


## Best practices

- **Author the procedure by observing someone perform it, not by asking them to describe it.** — People describe the version they believe they follow. The steps they have automated into muscle memory are the ones they forget to mention, and those are the ones a stranger cannot guess. The gap between the described process and the observed process is typically the whole of the error rate.

- **Validate by having someone who has never performed the task complete it unaided, and log every question they ask.** — The questions are the defect list, and they cluster — three or four gaps generate most of the traffic. An SOP its author can follow proves nothing, because the author is supplying the missing steps from memory without noticing.

- **Trigger review from system and organisational change events; use the calendar only as a backstop.** — The annual review of an unchanged procedure is theatre, and it consumes the review budget that the procedure whose platform was replaced in March actually needed. Calendar review also manufactures the most damaging artefact in document control: a record saying 'reviewed, no change' for a procedure that changed in every particular.

- **Distinguish steps that get the work done from steps that exist to satisfy a control.** — Process improvement removes the steps that slow the work down, and the control steps are exactly those — they produce evidence and advance nothing. An editor who cannot see which is which either removes a control or refuses to remove anything, and both outcomes are bad.

- **Document what to do when the happy path fails, not only the happy path.** — The happy path is learned in a week. The exception path is the entire reason the one experienced person is still needed, and removing that dependency was the point of writing the procedure at all. A procedure covering only the happy path has documented the easy half and claimed the hard one.

- **Carry the version on the document the performer actually opens.** — 'Which version did they follow' is the only version question ever asked, and it is asked after something has gone wrong. A register that knows the answer and a copy that does not is a register that cannot help.

- **Cross-train a second performer while the process is still routine, not after it becomes critical.** — Bus factor is discovered at the worst available moment by construction: the day the person is unavailable is not correlated with the day the task is due, so eventually it coincides. The training costs two days when nothing is on fire and cannot be bought at any price when something is.

- **Retire a superseded procedure by removing it from where people look, and record why.** — A superseded procedure still in the shared drive is followed by exactly the population the supersession was meant to protect. And a retirement with no recorded reason returns within three years, reconstructed from memory by someone who was not there.

- **Make the procedure a deliverable of the leaver process, with the successor as its tester.** — It is the only window where the tribal knowledge is both present and structurally motivated to be transferred. Documentation written afterwards by the successor records what they could reconstruct from the artefacts, which is the happy path and nothing else.

- **Watch step_count and observed cycle time together over time.** — Steps accumulate after incidents and are never removed. When the count rises and the observed duration does not, people have started skimming — and skimming selects against the steps that do not help finish the work, which are the controls that were added after the incidents.



## Anti-patterns

- **A procedure describing what the auditor expects rather than what the team does.** — tempting because It was authored in the fortnight before a certification audit, by someone from the quality function rather than from the team, and it passed. Passing confirmed the method, so it was used again.
 Instead: Author from observation, then close the gap between the observed process and the control requirement deliberately, as a change with a date, an owner and a training implication.

- **A review record reading 'reviewed, no change' every year for a procedure whose underlying systems have been replaced twice.** — tempting because The review is an obligation with a date attached and no test attached. Ticking it is cheap and indistinguishable, in the record, from doing it properly.
 Instead: Require the reviewer to name what they checked and against whom — observed execution, performer walkthrough, output sampling — and let owner_assertion be recorded honestly when that is what happened. A set that is 80% owner-asserted is a useful and uncomfortable fact.

- **A procedure whose operative steps are screenshots of an interface that no longer exists.** — tempting because Screenshots are the fastest way to write a clear procedure. They were correct the day they were taken, and nothing about the document announces that they have stopped being correct.
 Instead: Name fields and menu paths in text; use screenshots for orientation and never for the operative step. Track tooling_referenced as structured data so a rename invalidates the affected procedures explicitly rather than silently.

- **Written by the only person who performs it, and never run by anyone else.** — tempting because They are the only one who knows, so they are the obvious author, and asking anybody else to test it costs a day the function does not have.
 Instead: A stranger executes it once before publication and their questions are treated as defects against the document rather than as gaps in the stranger.

- **A document stating what must be achieved, with no steps, filed as an SOP.** — tempting because Writing the rule takes a day and writing the steps takes a fortnight. The rule reads as authoritative, satisfies the request, and closes the action.
 Instead: Apply the discriminator: could a competent stranger complete the task from this alone? If not, file it as a policy and leave the SOP gap open and visible.

- **Three teams run three versions and each believes theirs is the SOP.** — tempting because One team hit a case the central procedure did not cover, forked a copy to fix it, and got on with the work. That was the fastest correct action available at the time.
 Instead: Make forking legitimate and visible — a variant register with an owner and a merge-back date. Unrecorded forking is guaranteed; the only choice available is whether it is recordable.

- **A procedure gains a step after every incident and never loses one.** — tempting because Adding a step is the cheapest visible response to an incident. Removing one requires arguing that a control is unnecessary, and owning that argument the next time something goes wrong.
 Instead: Every added step carries an owner and a review date. Watch step_count against observed duration; when the two stop moving together, people are skipping.

- **The procedure is documented after the leaver has gone, by the person taking over, from the artefacts.** — tempting because Notice periods are consumed by live work, and the departing person is the least motivated author in the building. The successor is highly motivated and available.
 Instead: Handover is a leaver deliverable with the successor as tester, and the exception paths are a required section signed off before the last day.

- **Success is measured by procedures published, and the number only goes up.** — tempting because Coverage is countable, reportable and unambiguous. Fidelity is none of those things, so the metric that exists drives the behaviour.
 Instead: Report critical_process_coverage counting verified only, and publish drifted_share alongside it. Two numbers, and the second one has to be allowed to be ugly.

- `admin.obj.core.document` — requires (hard)
- `admin.obj.core.employee_record` — requires (hard)
- `admin.obj.core.policy` — enriches (soft)
- `admin.obj.core.compliance_obligation` — enriches (soft)
- `admin.obj.core.approval` — requires (soft)
- `admin.obj.core.request` — enriches (soft)
- `admin.obj.core.service_level` — enriches (soft)
- `admin.obj.core.audit_evidence` — enriches (soft)
- `admin.obj.core.contract` — invalidated_by (soft)
- `admin.obj.core.employee_record` — invalidated_by (hard)


## Inputs

- **document** — the controlled artefact: steps, version, approval block, review date
- **register** — document control register: owner, cycle, criticality, supersession chain
- **email** — questions asked about the procedure and review traffic
- **email** — who owes the next move on a review or an unanswered how-do-I
- **derived** — trajectory of conversation about the procedure
- **erp** — the transaction trail the procedure produces — sequence, timing, performer
- **telemetry** — system events showing the procedure being executed step by step
- **knowledge_base** — where the procedure is looked up, and how often
- **hris** — owner and performer employment status, joiners and leavers
- **meeting_transcript** — process walkthroughs and handover sessions
- **portal** — the request queue the procedure serves — cycle time against the written duration
- **manual_entry** — the owner's assertion that the procedure is current


## Outputs

- **`executable_by_a_stranger_bp`** Whether someone who has never done this task could complete it from the document today. The object's whole reason for existing, expressed as one number. → L4.reasoning_unit, L4.decision_maker
- **`drift_days`** Days since the document was last tested against practice, weighted by how fast the systems underneath it are moving. → L4.reasoning_unit, L6.learning_unit
- **`bus_factor`** How many people can run this. The number an SOP set exists to raise, and the one nobody reports. → L4.reasoning_unit, L5.execution_planning
- **`continuity_risk`** What stops working, and when, if the named owner leaves. Feeds leaver planning rather than document control. → L4.decision_maker, L5.execution_planning
- **`verification_plan`** Which procedures to observe next, ordered by criticality times verification age rather than by review date. → L5.execution_planning
- **`version_in_force`** The wording binding on a given date. The only version question that ever gets asked, and it gets asked after something has gone wrong. → L4.decision_maker
- **`who_to_ask`** The named fallback when the procedure does not cover the case. Routing, not documentation — and the honest answer where readability is tribal_only. → L5.communication_planning, L5.2.channel_planner


## Events

- **`sop.published`** Procedure Published
- **`sop.verified`** Verified Against Practice
- **`sop.drift_suspected`** Drift Suspected — invalidates drift_state, time_to_first_success_minutes, expected_duration_minutes
- **`sop.maintenance_overdue`** Maintenance Overdue
- **`sop.owner_departed`** Procedure Owner Departed — invalidates owner_ref, single_point_of_failure, last_verified_against_practice_at, exception_path_documented
- **`sop.tooling_changed`** Underlying System Changed — invalidates tooling_referenced, drift_state, time_to_first_success_minutes
- **`sop.deviation_recorded`** Deviation Recorded
- **`sop.variant_discovered`** Local Variant Discovered — invalidates drift_state, step_count
- **`sop.superseded`** Procedure Superseded


## Actions

- **Watch someone perform it** (human) — The gemba walk. Costs an hour and catches the steps the performer has stopped consciously noticing, which are the steps that are missing from the document.
- **Have someone who has never done it run it** (human) — Every question they have to ask is a defect. An SOP its author can follow proves only that the author is carrying the missing steps in their head.
- **Schedule the next verification** (system) — Ordered by criticality times verification age, not by review date. The two orderings are almost unrelated.
- **Reissue with a new version** (human) — For any change to a step, its order or its performer. Silent step edits destroy the only useful property of versioning.
- **Cross-train a second performer** (human) — The only action here that changes the underlying risk rather than describing it. Everything else improves the document.
- **Withdraw superseded copies** (system) — From every location performers look, not from the register. The register is read by the people who were never going to follow the old version.
- **Record a deviation** (agent) — At the time, with performer and reason. A deviation reconstructed at audit is a story about a deviation.
- **Mark which steps are controls** (human) — Makes the procedure safely editable. Until it is done, every efficiency review is a coin toss between removing a control and removing nothing.
- **Capture the procedure during a leaver handover** (human) — With the successor as the tester and the exception paths as the required section. The one window in which the tribal knowledge is both present and motivated to leave.
- **Retire the procedure** (human) — With the reason recorded. A procedure retired without a reason returns in three years, reconstructed from memory and worse.


## Evidence

- **telemetry** · 9000 bp — System events showing the procedure being executed. The only evidence that does not depend on somebody's account of their own work, and the only source that can prove a step was skipped.
- **erp** · 8500 bp — The transaction trail the procedure leaves. The real process read backwards from what it produced — usually a surprise to the person who wrote the document.
- **register** · 8000 bp — Document control register: owner, version, criticality, review date. Authoritative on currency and completely silent on fidelity, which is the confusion this whole object exists to break.
- **document** · 7500 bp — The controlled artefact. Proves what was written and the date it was approved. Proves nothing whatever about what was done.
- **hris** · 7500 bp — Owner and performer employment status. The source that turns a leaver date into a continuity risk before rather than after the handover window closes.
- **meeting_transcript** · 6500 bp — A walkthrough with the performer. Better than reading the document and worse than watching the work — people describe the version they believe they follow.
- **knowledge_base** · 6000 bp — Access and search data. Weak on content, uniquely strong on the one question the register cannot answer: does anyone open this.
- **attestation** · 5500 bp — A performer's recorded confirmation that they follow it. Evidence of willingness and of distribution. Not evidence of practice, and treating it as such is how attestation theatre starts.
- **email** · 4500 bp — Questions asked about the task. Diagnostic of the document's defects rather than of its content — and the defect list is more useful than the content review.
- **portal** · 5500 bp — The request queue the procedure serves. Cycle time is an independent check on the written duration and needs nobody's cooperation.
- **manual_entry** · 3000 bp — Someone asserted this is the process. The weakest link in the chain and, in every organisation, the most common one.
- **derived** · 3000 bp — Inferred from graph shape and traffic. Corroborating only, never sole grounds.


## Metrics

- **stranger_execution_success_rate** (percent) — Share of first attempts by someone who has never performed the task that complete correctly and unaided. The only measure of an SOP that cannot be gamed by the author.
- **verification_age** (days) — Time since the document was last compared to observed practice. Almost universally unmeasured, because almost nobody records the second date.
- **drifted_share** (percent) — Share of the procedure set at suspected_drift or worse. Reported honestly it is alarming; that is the point.
- **bus_factor** (count) — Distinct people who have executed the procedure end to end. The number the whole exercise exists to move, and the one nobody puts on a dashboard.
- **questions_per_execution** (count) — Questions asked per run. Read against access counts — zero questions means either an excellent procedure or an unopened one.
- **cycle_time_vs_documented_duration** (percent) — Observed against written. Divergence in either direction is drift; faster is the dangerous direction and looks like a win on every dashboard.
- **critical_process_coverage** (percent) — Share of business_critical and above processes with a verified, non-tribal procedure. Counts verified only — presumed_current does not qualify.
- **time_from_change_to_reissue** (days) — System or process change to updated wording in the performers' hands. The window in which the document is known-wrong and still being followed by joiners.
- **orphaned_procedure_count** (count) — Procedures with no owner, no executions and no traffic. Every procedure set has them and no report lists them.

## Examples

- **Month-end supplier payment run** _(typical)_ — 22 steps, two approval gates, one performer, run twelve times a year. Classic single point of failure — well documented, never executed by anyone else, and the exception path (supplier not on the approved list) lives entirely in the performer's head.
- **New starter account provisioning runbook** _(typical)_ — Executed weekly, high visibility, drifts fastest of anything in the set because the identity platform ships changes continuously. The procedure most likely to be screenshot-based and therefore most likely to be a museum.
- **Board pack assembly** _(edge)_ — Six executions a year, one performer, criticality business_critical. Too infrequent to build muscle memory and too infrequent to justify cross-training, which is why it is always the process discovered to be undocumented three days before a board meeting.
- **Fire evacuation procedure** _(edge)_ — safety_critical, never executed in anger, verified only by drill. The drill IS the verification and is the only evidence that exists — which makes verification_method the entire quality of the procedure.
- **Travel and expense policy filed under SOPs** _(misclassification)_ — States per-night caps and eligibility. No steps, no performer, no trigger. It is admin.obj.core.policy, and filing it here closes the SOP gap on paper while leaving it open in fact.
- **A pinned Slack checklist with no owner and no version** _(misclassification)_ — Has the appearance of a procedure and none of its properties. It is tribal knowledge with a URL — genuinely useful, and it should be recorded as readability = tribal_only rather than counted as coverage.
- **Handling a distressed complainant** _(counterexample)_ — A decision, not a procedure. Written as steps it will be followed literally by exactly the person least equipped to notice that this case needs something else. Principles and worked examples are the correct artefact and the honest answer.
- **Statutory annual return preparation** _(typical)_ — obligation_ref populated, criticality regulated. Drift here does not produce rework — it produces an evidence trail describing a process nobody performed, which is the finding rather than the error.
- **A procedure for a system decommissioned last year** _(edge)_ — drift_state = obsolete, review date current, owner still listed. Scores green on every document-control report in existence. It is retired by removal, not by correction, and until someone removes it search will keep offering it to joiners.

## Metadata

owner **Admin** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional** · completeness **complete**


> Five of thirteen patterns are executable today: an overdue maintenance commitment, a maintenance promise abandoned for a quarter, graph orphaning, a knowledge bottleneck read off reply cadence, and a collapse in traffic. That is an honest ceiling rather than a thin first pass — the shipped substrate can see promises made about a procedure and conversation around it, and can see nothing at all about whether the procedure is being followed. The standout Layer 1/2 asks are sop_executed and derived.performer_diversity. Performer diversity is the only number that says whether writing the SOP achieved anything, it is trivial arithmetic once execution records exist, and nothing today reaches the systems where procedures are actually executed. Second is version identity on the copy rather than the master (document.version), without which the object's central failure — the joiner following a stale version — is undetectable by construction. The boundary with admin.obj.core.policy is deliberate and load-bearing in both directions. A policy states what must be true and is self-imposed; an SOP states how and is one of several possible methods. Filing a policy as an SOP closes the coverage gap on paper and leaves it open in fact, and it is the commonest misclassification in this subdomain.
